description:
The name of Monda Castle likely derives from "El Mundat," a fortress built in the 9th century by Omar Ben Hafsún to strengthen his positions against the armies of Córdoba's last emirs. The structure was destroyed and rebuilt in the 11th century by the Hammudids. The polygonal tower that survives today was raised by the Almohads in the 12th century, and is typologically similar to the Torre del Oro in Seville. In the 14th century, the Nasrid dynasty — the same dynasty that built the Alhambra in Granada — reformed the polygonal tower, cladding it with a square-plan tower.

Today the castle operates as a 4-star boutique hotel, in the town center of Monda, at the heart of Málaga province.

The tower's documented typological link to Seville's Torre del Oro, both built during the Almohad period, gives Monda a specific architectural pedigree connecting it to one of Andalusia's most recognizable medieval monuments.

The site's successive rebuilding under three different Muslim dynasties — the original 9th-century fortress, the 11th-century Hammudid reconstruction, and the 12th-century Almohad tower later reclad by the Nasrids — gives Monda a layered architectural history spanning five centuries of al-Andalus rule.

The castle's position within Monda's own town center gives guests staying here a genuinely integrated historic setting, rather than an isolated hilltop or rural estate.
